svg.aria-label: Animated float4 loads of A’s tile. Every K step a block copies a 128 by 32 tile of A from global memory into shared memory. Loading one float per load, row 0 of the tile takes 32 loads; with float4, threads t0 to t7 each load 4 floats, so the same bytes take 8 loads, 4 times fewer, and B’s tile loads the same way. Aside: As is stored transposed, so t0’s 4 values go down column 0, one row per k, t1’s 4 values continue down the same column, and t2 to t7 follow down to k = 31; the transpose only changes where values land. Rows continue to k = 31 and columns to row 127 of A.
svg.text: Loading A’s tile: 1 float vs. 4 floats per load
As, stored transposed: one row per k, one column per row of A
shown: rows 0–15 of A (of 128) across, k = 0–7 (of 32) down
t2–t7 continue down column 0 to k = 31
Every K step, a block copies A’s 128×32 tile from global memory into shared memory.
Before: each load moves one float, so row 0 alone takes 32 of them.
With float4, each thread moves 4 neighboring floats in one load.
Fewer loads to issue for the same tile: that is the whole speedup of this step.
Aside: As is stored transposed, so t0’s 4 values run down column 0, one row per k.
Wide loads cut global loads 4×; the transpose only changes where the values land.
